source_text: Deos non esse quos colit vulgus hinc notum est. Reges olim fuerunt, qui ob regalem memoriam coli apud suos postmodum etiam in morte coeperunt. Inde illis instituta templa, inde, ad defunctorum vultus per imaginem detinendos, expressa simulacra; et immolabant hostias, et dies festos dando honore celebrabant. Inde posteris facta sunt sacra, quae primis fuerant assumpta solatia. Et videamus an stet haec apud singulos veritas. Melicertes et Leucothea praecipitantur in maria, et fiunt postmodum maris numina. Castores alternis moriuntur ut vivant. Aesculapius ut in Deum surgat fulminatur. Hercules ut hominem exuat Oeteis ignibus concrematur. Apollo Admeti pecus pavit. Laomedonti muros Neptunus instituit, nec mercedem operis infelix structor accepit. Antrum Jovis in Creta visitur, et sepulchrum ejus ostenditur, et ab eo Saturnum fugatum esse manifestum est. Inde Latium de latebra ejus nomen accepit. Hic litteras imprimere, hic signare nummos in Italia primus instituit: inde aerarium Saturni vocatur. Et rusticitatis hic cultor fuit: inde falcem ferens senex pingitur. Hunc fugatum hospitio Janus exceperat; de cujus nomine Janiculum dictum est, et mensis Januarius institutus est. Ipse bifrons exprimitur, quod, in medio constitutus, annum incipientem pariter et recedentem spectare videatur. Mauri vero manifeste reges colunt, nec ullo velamento hoc nomen obtexunt. Inde per gentes et provincias singulas varia deorum religio mutatur, dum non unus ab omnibus deus colitur, sed propria cuique majorum suorum cultura servatur. Hoc ita Alexander Magnus insigni volumine ad matrem suam scribit metu suae potestatis proditum sibi de diis hominibus a sacerdote secretum, quod majorum et regum memoria servata sit, inde colendi et sacrificandi ritus inoleverit. Si autem aliquando dii nati sunt, cur non hodieque nascuntur? nisi si forte Jupiter senuit, aut partus in Junone defecit. Cur vero deos putas pro Romanis posse, quos videas nihil pro suis adversus eorum arma valuisse? Romanorum enim vernaculos deos novimus. Est Romulus pejerante Proculo deus factus, et Picus, et Tiberinus, et Pilumnus, et Consus, quem Deum fraudis vel ut consiliorum deum, coli Romulus voluit postquam in raptum Sabinarum perfidia provenit. Deam quoque Cloacinam Tatius et invenit et coluit, Pavorem Hostilius atque Pallorem. Mox a nescio quo Febris dedicata, et Acca et Flora meretrices. [Interdum vero deorum vocabula apud Romanos finguntur, ut sit apud illos et Viduus deus, qui anima corpus viduet, qui quasi feralis et funebris intra muros non habetur; et nihilominus, quia extorris factus, damnatur potius Romana religione, quam colitur. Est et Scansus ab ascensibus dictus, et Forculus a foribus, et a liminaribus Limentinus, et Cardea a cardinibus et ab orbitatibus Orbona]. Hi dii Romani. Caeterum Mars Thracius, et Jupiter Creticus, et Juno vel Argiva vel Samia vel Poena, et Diana Taurica, et deorum mater Idaea, et Aegyptia portenta, non numina: quae utique si quid potestatis habuissent, sua ac suorum regna servassent. Plane sunt apud Romanos et victi penates, quos Aeneas profugus advexit. Est et Venus calva, multo hic turpius calva quam apud Homerum vulnerata.
pass_a_gloss: It is known that the gods whom the common people worship do not exist. Formerly, there were kings who, on account of their royal memory, began to be worshiped by their people even after death. From this, temples were established for them, and images were made to preserve their likeness after death. They also offered sacrifices and celebrated festivals in their honor. From this, sacred rites were created for posterity, which were initially taken up as consolations for the first ones. Let us see if this truth stands among individuals. Melicertes and Leucothea were thrown into the sea and later became sea gods. The Castors die alternately so that they may live. Aesculapius was struck by lightning so that he might rise to be a god. Hercules was cremated in the fires of Oeta so that he might shed his human form. Apollo herded Admetus' cattle. Neptune built walls for Laomedon, but the unfortunate builder did not receive payment for his work. The cave of Jupiter on Crete is visited, and his tomb is shown, and it is clear that he fled from Saturn. From this, Latium received its name from his hiding place. He was the first to introduce letters and coinage in Italy, and from this, the treasury of Saturn is named. He was also a cultivator of the land, and therefore, he is depicted as an old man carrying a sickle. This fugitive was received by Janus, and from his name, the Janiculum is named, and the month of January is established. He himself is depicted as two-faced because, being in the middle, he seems to look equally at the beginning and end of the year. The Moors, indeed, openly worship kings, and they do not conceal this name with any veil. From this, the religion of the gods varies among the nations and provinces, since not one god is worshiped by all, but each people preserves its own ancestral culture. Alexander the Great writes to his mother in a remarkable volume, revealing a secret told to him by a priest about the gods, that the memory of ancestors and kings has been preserved, and from this, the rites of worship and sacrifice have developed. But if the gods were ever born, why are they not born today? Unless perhaps Jupiter has grown old or childbirth has ceased in Juno. Why do you think the gods can do anything for the Romans when you see that they have not been able to do anything for their own people against the Roman arms? We know the Roman gods are homegrown. Romulus became a god by the perjury of Proculus, as did Picus, Tiberinus, Pilumnus, and Consus, whom Romulus wanted to be worshiped as the god of fraud or counsel after his treachery in the abduction of the Sabine women. Tatius also found and worshiped the goddess Cloacina, and Hostilius worshiped Fear and Pallor. Later, Fever was dedicated by someone, and Acca and Flora, prostitutes, were also worshiped. Sometimes, indeed, the names of gods are fabricated among the Romans, such as the god Viduus, who separates the soul from the body, and who, like a funeral god, is not kept within the walls. Nevertheless, because he was banished, he is condemned rather than worshiped by Roman religion. There is also Scansus, named from stairs, and Forculus from doors, and Limentinus from thresholds, and Cardea from hinges, and Orbona from orbits. These are the Roman gods. Moreover, Mars is Thracian, and Jupiter is Cretan, and Juno is either Argive or Samian or Carthaginian, and Diana is Taurian, and the mother of the gods is from Ida, and the Egyptian portents are not divine powers. If they had any power, they would have preserved their own kingdoms and those of their people. Clearly, there are also conquered household gods among the Romans, which Aeneas brought as a refugee. There is also Venus, who is bald, and here she is more shamefully bald than when she was wounded in Homer's account.
